opus-5.5.text:
I think we're in the middle of a pretty fundamental shift. For a long time, the dominant way of interacting with AI was the chat box: you ask a question, it gives you an answer, and you go back and forth. That paradigm works well when the task is essentially information retrieval or short-form generation. But once agents start doing real productivity work, like writing and running code, operating software, or handling a multi-step workflow that takes hours, the chat box starts to feel like the wrong interface.

The first change I see is that the unit of interaction is moving from a "turn" to a "task." Instead of supervising every step, you delegate a goal, and the agent works on it asynchronously. So the human's role shifts from operator to something more like a manager or a reviewer. You set the intent, define what "done" looks like, and check the result. That sounds simple, but it changes a lot. The hard part is no longer how to phrase the prompt. It's how to specify the task well, and how to verify the output efficiently.

The second change is around trust and checkpoints. When an agent runs for a long time, you can't read every line it produces. So the interaction needs natural points where the agent surfaces what matters: "I made this decision, here's why," or "I'm uncertain here, can you confirm?" Good agents will know when to interrupt you and when not to. Interrupting too much makes them useless; interrupting too little makes them dangerous. Getting that balance right is as much a product problem as a model problem.

Third, I think context becomes the real interface. In productivity scenarios, the agent's value depends heavily on how much it understands about your environment: your codebase, your documents, your preferences, your past decisions. Over time, interaction becomes less about explaining things from scratch every time and more about the agent accumulating a working memory of you and your work. That's when it starts to feel like a colleague rather than a tool.

And finally, from the model side, this puts different demands on what we train for. It's not just about being smart in a single response. It's about long-horizon reliability, using tools correctly, recovering from its own mistakes, and staying coherent over a long trajectory. Those capabilities are what make the new interaction mode possible. So I'd say the interface evolution and the model capability evolution are really happening together. Each one pulls the other forward.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the interaction model is going to shift from "chat" to something closer to "delegation."

Right now most people still interact with agents through a conversational window. You type, it responds, you type again. That works fine for coding, because programmers are used to specifying things precisely and are willing to iterate in text. But as agents move into broader productivity work, that model starts to break down. A product manager, a lawyer, an operations person, they don't want to sit in a dialogue box babysitting the model. They want to hand off a task the way they'd hand it to a capable colleague, and then get back a result, or at most a few targeted questions.

So I see a few concrete changes.

First, the unit of interaction gets bigger. Instead of a message, it becomes a task, sometimes one that runs for hours or days. That means the agent has to be good at working without you, and good at knowing when it actually needs you. The hard part isn't capability on a single step, it's judgment about when to stop and ask versus when to keep going. If it asks too much, it's useless. If it asks too little, it does the wrong thing confidently.

Second, the agent needs to live where the work lives. A lot of productivity isn't in a chat app, it's in documents, spreadsheets, browsers, internal tools, email. The agent needs to be able to see and act in those environments, not just describe what you should do there. Context becomes the real bottleneck. The model may be smart enough, but if it doesn't know what your team decided last week or what the customer said in that thread, it will produce something plausible and wrong.

Third, trust gets built in layers. Early on, people will want to review everything. Over time, for specific kinds of tasks, they'll let the agent act with less oversight, the same way you'd gradually give a new hire more autonomy. So the interface has to make it easy to see what the agent did and why, and easy to roll back. Transparency isn't a nice-to-have, it's what allows autonomy to grow.

And finally, I think the interaction becomes less about prompting skill. Today there's still a gap between people who know how to "talk to" a model and people who don't. For agents to really spread, that gap has to close. The agent should take some responsibility for understanding a vague request, asking a good clarifying question, and figuring out the intent, rather than putting the burden on the user to specify everything.

So in short, fewer conversations, more delegation; deeper integration into real tools; trust earned incrementally; and less dependence on the user being an expert at talking to AI. That's the direction I expect it to go.

astra-6.text:
I think the interaction will gradually shift from giving instructions for every step to expressing a goal and working with the agent toward it. Today, you often have to explain the task, supply the context, and keep checking the output. In broader productivity scenarios, an agent needs to understand more of the context, carry out parts of the work, and recognize when it should come back to you.

That makes knowing when to ask a question very important. If it asks about everything, you’re still doing the work of managing every step. If it makes too many assumptions, you can lose trust in it. The interaction has to find a balance: act independently where the intent is clear, and involve the person where a decision really matters.

I also don’t think everything will happen through a chat window. Sometimes the most useful interaction will be a change in a document, a proposed next step, or a result you can inspect directly. People should be able to understand what the agent has done and redirect it easily. As that becomes more reliable, I think we’ll spend less effort operating software and more effort deciding what we want to accomplish.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we’ll move from asking AI questions to working with it toward a goal. Today, people often have to break a task into steps, write prompts, and move information between tools. As agents become more capable, you’ll be able to explain what you want to accomplish, and the agent will help plan the work, carry it out, and bring you back in when a decision needs your judgment.

But the interaction shouldn’t disappear entirely. In productivity scenarios, people need to understand what the agent is doing, correct its assumptions, and control consequential actions. So I expect a more collaborative pattern: sometimes you delegate, sometimes you work together, and sometimes the agent asks a short question because something is ambiguous.

The important shift is that users shouldn’t have to become experts at prompting. The system should become better at understanding their context and intent, while making its own limits clear. That’s what will make agents useful in everyday work.
